title: 道德經 第二十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 25, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 65. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 25 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 象元 (Imaging the Origin). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
有物混成，
先天地生。

morph.gloss: there is — the existential verb, standing at the head with no subject before it
run together, all of a piece — what water and mud become when stirred until neither can be picked out
prior to, earlier than — a word of position doing duty as a verb
heaven and earth — the cosmos taken as one pair

sentences.l:
There is a thing run together and complete,
before heaven-and-earth, born.
sentences.i: Something there is, all of a piece and entire, that came to life before heaven and earth did.
sentences.n: 有物 — 'there is a thing'. The book will not usually allow the Way to be a thing at all: chapter 14 sent it back to 無物, 'no-thing'. So the flat opening here is deliberate and a little shocking, as if the nameless could be pointed at. In 混成, 混 is a stative verb standing before 成 with nothing to mark it as adverbial — 'blurredly complete'; Wang Bi glosses it as blurred so that one cannot get hold of it and know it, and yet the ten thousand things are brought to completion through it. 先 is a noun of position ('the front, the earlier') doing duty as a verb governing what follows — a shift nothing on the page marks, and one this chapter makes again and again: 字 'a style-name' becomes 'to give a style-name', 法 'a standard' becomes 'to take as one's standard', and 大 'great' becomes 'a great one'. Also worth hearing: 成 chéng and 生 shēng close the two lines and rhymed in Old Chinese — a rhyme Mandarin happens to have kept.

sentences.t:
寂兮寥兮，
獨立而不改，

morph.gloss: the verse particle: a breath and a lift, with nothing to translate
empty and wide open — space with nothing standing in it
and — here simply linking two things said of the same subject, not the adversative 'and yet' it is in the next line
to alter, to become other than it was

sentences.l:
Silent! — and empty! —
alone it stands and does not alter,
sentences.i: Soundless, without bulk, it stands by itself and is never altered;
sentences.n: 兮 you have carried since chapter 15: it means nothing at all, only breath. 寂 and 寥 are both denials — no sound, no bulk — and between them they say that this thing offers the ear and the eye nothing to catch; later Chinese glued the two into 寂寥, still the word for a desolate emptiness. 獨立 here is not the modern 'independence' it later became: 獨 'alone' simply describes the standing.

sentences.t:
周行而不殆，
可以為天下母。

morph.gloss: to go, to travel (xíng; háng is 'a row, a rank')
and yet — adversative here: for all that going, still no danger
to come into danger, to be imperilled — the word of chapter 16's 沒身不殆
can, may — and what follows it reads passively
by that, thereby (the object is left out)
to be taken for, to serve as — wéi, the 'act as' reading
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it

sentences.l:
goes the whole round and yet comes to no harm.
By that it may be taken for the mother of all-under-heaven.
sentences.i: it travels the full circuit and is never brought into danger, and may be counted the mother of all under heaven.
sentences.n: 可以 is not yet the modern single word 'may': it is 可 'can' plus 以 'by that means', with the means left unstated because the whole line before it is the means. Wang Bi glosses 周行 as reaching everywhere with no place left out, and 不殆 as never being brought into danger by the going. Textual note: the Mawangdui silk manuscripts read 天地母, 'the mother of heaven and earth', where our text has 天下母, 'the mother of all under heaven' — one character, and it shifts the claim from the world of men to the cosmos. The Guodian bamboo slips, older still, do not have 周行而不殆 at all.

morph.gloss: name — the name proper, given at birth

sentences.l: I do not know its name,
sentences.n: 吾 'I' is rare in this book and always worth stopping at. In chapter 16 it was watching rather than telling; in chapter 4 it said very nearly this — 吾不知誰之子, 'I do not know whose child it is'. The admission is the argument: what was there before heaven and earth cannot have been named by anything that came after.

morph.gloss: to give a style-name to — the noun 字, the name a man takes at his capping, used here as a verb
it — the object pronoun, not the genitive 'of'

sentences.l: I style-name it, and say: the Way.
sentences.i: so I give it a style-name and call it the Way.
sentences.n: This is the chapter's finest stroke and it vanishes in translation. A man of this period had two names: his 名, given by his father at birth, which only his elders and his ruler used; and his 字, the style-name taken at capping, which is what everyone else called him by. The text has just said it does not know the thing's 名 — so it does not presume to give one. It gives a 字 instead: a name for others to use, not the name that says what a thing is. 之 here is the object pronoun 'it'; in chapter 1 the same character was the genitive 'of', and only position tells them apart.

morph.gloss: by force, straining to — read qiǎng, 'to compel', not qiáng 'strong'
for it — the pronoun again, now the one the name is made for

sentences.l: Straining, I make a name for it and say: Great.
sentences.i: and if I must force a name on it, I say: the Great.
sentences.n: 強為之名 is the twin of chapter 15's 強為之容, 'one forcibly makes a likeness of it' — the same admission that the words are being pushed past what they can carry. 強 is read qiǎng, the verb 'to compel', standing where English would put an adverb. And 大 is no more a name than 道 was: the next three lines set about showing that it will not hold still.

morph.gloss: to pass on, to go away — said of a river running off and of the dead

sentences.n: A chain of definitions, A 曰 B, B 曰 C, each link picking up the last word: the same figure as chapter 16's 歸根曰靜，是謂復命, and 曰 does the same work here that it did there — not 'say' but 'is called'. Wang Bi glosses 逝 flatly as 行, 'to move on', and reads it as a refusal to sit still inside the one great body — the greatness is not a place but a going.

morph.gloss: to turn back, to come round again — the same word later written 返

sentences.l:
passing-on is called far-going;
far-going is called turning back.
sentences.i: what passes on goes far, and what has gone far turns back.
sentences.n: 遠 yuǎn and 反 fǎn belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group (the 元 group), and in Mandarin they are still close enough to hear as a half-rhyme; 逝 stands outside that group and never chimed with them. 反 is 'to turn back', the same word later given a walking element and written 返; the turn is this book's physics, stated bare in chapter 40. Notice that the chain has quietly reversed itself: greatness goes out, going out becomes distance, and distance becomes the road home.

sentences.t:
故道大，
天大，
地大，
王亦大。

morph.gloss: the king — read wáng, the noun; wàng is the verb 'to reign'

sentences.i: So the Way is great, heaven is great, earth is great — and the king too is great.
sentences.n: Four predications and not a verb 'to be' among them: 道大 is simply 'Way | great'. The fourth member is the surprise, and the book means it — the ruler is where the Way reaches human affairs, which is why so much of this book reads as advice to a prince. A good many editions read 人亦大, 'man too is great', which agrees better with the ladder at the end of the chapter, where it is 人 'man' and not 王 'the king' who takes earth for a model. The mismatch is old and unsettled; our edition prints 王 here and in the next line, so we do too.

morph.gloss: a bounded ground, a marked-off expanse — the character is walled territory
within (zhōng; zhòng is the verb 'to hit the mark')
great ones — the adjective now standing as a noun, with nothing to mark the change

sentences.l: Within the bounds there are four great ones,
sentences.n: 域 is ground with an edge to it, a walled territory — an odd container for something the chapter has just called prior to heaven and earth, and Wang Bi has to work to keep the Way inside it. And 大, an adjective in each of the four lines above, is a noun here: 'great ones'. Nothing on the page marks the change; the numeral in front of it does all the work.

morph.gloss: to occupy, to take up a place in
a fused word, 於 'in' + 之 'them' — 'therein'; it can only close a clause

sentences.l: and the king occupies one of them, therein.
sentences.i: and the king is one of the four.
sentences.n: 焉 is two words in one character, 於 'in' plus 之 'it', which is why it never appears anywhere but the end of its clause. You met the graph in chapter 15 (豫焉) doing a quite different job, as a descriptive suffix turning a word into a manner — the work 然 does — one character, two unrelated uses. 居 is the verb of chapter 2's 功成而弗居, 'does not lay claim to it'; here it is the neutral 'holds a place'.

sentences.t:
人法地，
地法天，
天法道，
道法自然。

morph.gloss: to take as one's model — the noun 'law, pattern' used as a verb
so of itself — what a thing is when nothing is done to it

sentences.l:
Man takes earth for his model,
earth takes heaven for its model,
heaven takes the Way for its model,
and the Way takes for its model what is so of itself.
sentences.i: Man is patterned on earth, earth on heaven, heaven on the Way — and the Way on what is so of itself.
sentences.n: 法 is 'law, standard' pressed into service as a verb: to take a thing for one's rule. The ladder climbs by handing the last rung's second word up to be the next rung's first, exactly as chapter 16's did — and then the top rung refuses to climb. 自然 is not a fifth and higher thing standing above the Way. It is 'self-so', and the line says that the Way has nothing to copy: it is its own being-so. Wang Bi puts it just that way — the Way does not go against 自然 and so obtains its own nature; 自然, he says, is a word with no name behind it, the last thing that can be said. Notice also who begins the ladder: 人, 'man', where four lines earlier the fourth great one was 王, 'the king'.
